item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] 'Non-lethal': How India and Israel's brutal use of pellet guns spread worldwide
item.description:
'Non-lethal': How India and Israel's brutal use of pellet guns spread worldwide

Submitted by Anuradha Bhasin on Wed, 09/23/2026 - 11:36
The real danger isn't in how these lethal technologies, including pellet guns, are exported and shared; the greater peril is in the precedent their use against civilian protesters sets
Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) supporters wave national flags a day after the resignation of India's Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan in Mumbai, India, 26 July 2026 (Punit Paranjape/AFP)
On

In July 2026, Amnesty International published a report Made in India: the supply of weapons and munitions to Israel. It found India shipped hundreds of thousands of weapon parts and munitions components to Israel throughout its Gaza offensive, and it warned the exports carry a "substantial risk" of contributing to what it calls Israel's "ongoing genocide".

The real danger isn't only in how these lethal technologies are exported and shared. The greater peril is in the wrong precedent their use against civilians sets.

A telling example is the use of pellet guns by police in Delhi to control a student’s march to the Indian parliament in protest against an examination leak scam, which injured at least 10 civilians, including a young man who may lose his vision forever. 

The journey of the use of pellet guns for crowd control from Kashmir to New Delhi reminds us that any battleground is always a testing ground. What gets legitimised in one place does not stay there. 

India introduced pellet guns in 2010 in Kashmir and framed it as a "non-lethal" or "less-lethal" weapon for crowd control. Between 2010 and 2019, 24 people were killed. Most casualties happened after their widespread use to control violent protests following the death of militant commander Burhan Wani, who was killed in an encounter in 2016. Between July 2016 and February 2019, metal pellets killed 18 people, blinded 139, and resulted in 2,942 injuries, of which 1,459 were serious eye injuries. 

A pellet gun is a .12-bore pump-action shotgun, normally used in bird hunting, that fires a cartridge loaded with several hundred metal pellets that disperse over a wide area rather than travelling as a single projectile.

Each cartridge holds up to several hundred small pellets. On firing, the pellets scatter outward in a wide spray at about 100-150 metres per second. Because of this spread, one shot can strike multiple people in a crowd at once.

In short, it doesn’t choose its target. It can hit anyone within that range. The enormous scale of injuries, even deaths, caused by pellets in Kashmir and the people they hit - a girl sitting by her window, a baby in her mother’s arms - made no distinction between allegedly violent protesters and those who just happened to be in the wrong place at the wrong moment.

Opening old wounds

The brutality of the pellet guns cannot be fully comprehended without understanding how the lives of the majority of the victims are scarred forever. 

Despite the "less-lethal" tag, the pellets are sharp enough to pierce the skin and stay embedded in the body, causing permanent pain in some cases. On occasion, they have caused permanent blindness. The psychological wounds they inflict are irreparable. There have also been cases of injuries resulting in deaths. 

Yet, the use of pellet guns in Kashmir was justified under a manufactured broad consensus built entirely through a security prism. 

The state embraced the weapon, framing it as "non-lethal", despite documentary evidence of hundreds blinded, scores killed, and many others permanently disabled. It invited no uproar or outrage. This nationwide tendency to see Kashmir as a state of exception has also encouraged a shameful mocking of its victims - the latest example being the forthcoming Bollywood film Chauhaan. 

It was used with the bland justification: terrorism, national security. This, even as there is no documentary evidence of the weapon ever being used against insurgents - only on civilian protesters. A security doctrine, borrowed from international playbooks, and built for a region on the pretext of insurgency, is now being exported. 

History of violence

Before its use in Delhi, pellet guns were used during the farmers’ protest and in Manipur. Their use in Delhi against protesting students evoked nationwide outrage, with the framing "they were students, not terrorists’". That framing never extends to the community the national imagination has already conflated with terrorists - Kashmir, Manipur and Punjab (whose farmers led the protests). The presumption of innocence isn't universal. It is assigned by identity.

Lethal weapon: How Bollywood's 'Chauhaan' trivialises the suffering of Kashmiris maimed by Indian forces
Read More »

Far more problematic is the state response that is still relying on old tactics of skirting questions about pellet injuries. It has moved from denial to deflection but no accountability.

As opposition leaders led by Congress, a party that ironically introduced pellet guns in 2010, are uniting and demanding answers to who ordered the pellet guns and why, India’s home minister Amit Shah has refused to attend parliament. 

Zero accountability automatically translates to a continuum of use of pellet guns or other weapons framed as "non-lethal’". In Kashmir, there is a documented record of young men killed when tear gas shells were directly aimed at their upper bodies in 2010. 

Even the Supreme Court has refused a total ban on the use of pellet guns and has deflected the question to examining the gaps between standard operating procedures and realities on the ground. The debate on whether lethal weapons can be used for crowd control is incomplete if restricted to these issues.

The debate also needs to take into account the impact of weapons that are projected as "non-lethal" or "less-lethal" but kill people nonetheless. It needs to weigh up the fact that a bad precedent travels from one geography to another and beyond borders.

Lethal export

Pellet guns have already travelled the globe. The United Kingdom is the first known country to have deployed shotguns with rubber and plastic pellets during the Troubles, the 30-year violent conflict in Northern Ireland, and inspired the United States police to adopt similar versions of the weapon for crowd control.

Pellet guns are just another demonstration of how quickly any state learns that civilians can be treated as acceptable targets once the first wrongful justification goes unchallenged

Pellet guns, along with other so-called "non-lethal" weapons, have been used with impunity in Palestine. Whether India borrowed this method of repression from Israel or not, the list of countries now using it to target their own citizens is growing.

In Chile in 2019, 230 people lost their vision. Bangladesh used it in 2024, killing 22 student protesters and blinding 400. They were used in the recent Iran protests, with at least 74 documented cases of pellet injuries in vital parts of the body. A man’s lung was damaged by 174 pellets tightly packed inside his right chest cavity.  

The pellet guns are just another demonstration of how quickly any state learns that civilians can be treated as acceptable targets once the first wrongful justification goes unchallenged.

Nuclear strikes may be a rare exception, but there are enough examples, like the use of white phosphorous and drone air strikes that reveal a brutal truth: what is used in one place doesn’t stay there; it travels wherever the next authority wants the same cover of impunity.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Council of Europe tells Serbia to implement judgement on Bahraini political prisoner
item.description:
Council of Europe tells Serbia to implement judgement on Bahraini political prisoner

Submitted by Oscar Rickett on Tue, 09/29/2026 - 07:00
Ahmed Jaafar Mohamed Ali was extradited from Serbia and has been in Bahrain's Jau Prison since 2022
Ahmed Jaafar Mohamed Ali has been held in Jau Prison since he was deported from Serbia in January 2022 (ADHRB)
Off

The Council of Europe has called on Serbia to implement a European Court of Human Rights judgement, which held that the Balkan country had violated the European Convention on Human Rights when it extradited a Bahraini activist seeking asylum. 

Ahmed Jaafar Mohamed Ali travelled to Serbia to seek asylum in November 2021 but was arrested by authorities there based on an Interpol red notice, which Ali’s lawyers say was unlawfully issued. 

The European Court of Human Rights issued an interim measure in January 2022 calling on Serbian authorities to refrain from extraditing Ali pending more information and particularly given the risk of torture or ill-treatment if he was returned. 

Three days later, campaigners say a private plane, chartered by United Arab Emirates-based Royal Jet Airlines, took Ali to Bahrain.

Ever since then the activist, who fled Bahrain in 2011 and then lived in Iran before travelling to Serbia, has been held in Bahrain’s Jau Prison on two life sentences.

Inside the prison, Ali says he has been beaten, denied medical treatment, had his faith insulted and held in solitary confinement. 

According to a recent call with fellow activists, a transcript of which was seen by Middle East Eye, Ali is currently being held in the prison’s Building Two, which houses violent offenders and those on serious drug charges.

Inside the building, the activist says these prisoners - acting on instruction from prison guards - beat and abuse him, creating a climate of fear that never lifts.

European ruling on Serbia 

In March 2025, the European Court of Human Rights ruled that Serbia had violated Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR) by extraditing Ali in defiance of an interim court block.

Article 3 of the convention safeguards against torture and inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment. The Serbian courts violated this when they failed to examine Ali’s complaint that he would face ill-treatment if sent back to Bahrain.

He is stuck in a severely overcrowded cell, has repeatedly had to resort to hunger strikes just to secure basic rights, and has been in and out of solitary confinement

- Sayed Ahmed Alwadaei, Bird

The ECHR ordered Serbia to pay 9,800 euros ($11,100), plus any tax chargeable and interest in the event of a default in payment. 

The Council of Europe’s Committee of Ministers says that, since the judgement, Serbia has placed a sum of money for Ali in a deposit account in a domestic court. 

However, the committee acknowledged his lawyers’ argument that there are “difficulties in complying with the conditions for the release of the funds given the exceptional nature of [Ali’s] situation” in Jau Prison.

The Council of Europe has said that Serbia should “co-operate with [Ali’s] representatives and the Secretariat to find solutions to enable the release of funds to take place without delay”.

Sayed Ahmed Alwadaei, director of advocacy at the Bahrain Institute for Rights and Democracy (Bird), told MEE that he had also been held in Building Two at Jau Prison, and that talking to Ali recently had brought back, in vivid detail, the suffering he had experienced there.   

“It was very hard to hear Ahmed describing to me the degrading conditions he is living in at Jau Prison. He is stuck in a severely overcrowded cell, has repeatedly had to resort to hunger strikes just to secure basic rights, and has been in and out of solitary confinement,” Alwadaei said.
 
“This decision is an important reminder that Serbia cannot simply take Bahrain’s assurances at face value. It must face the reality of what happened after Ahmed’s unlawful extradition and do everything it can to protect him.”

Political prisoners in Bahrain

Last year, Amnesty said that an estimated 322 political prisoners remained arbitrarily detained in Bahrain. 

Bahrain Grand Prix: Twenty years of dissent and sportswashing
Read More »

In the wake of the Arab Spring uprising of 2011, thousands of Bahrainis – mostly from the Sunni-ruled kingdom’s majority Shia population – were arrested and thrown in prison.

In 2024, Bahrain granted 1,500 prisoners royal pardons, and other similar moves have followed, but, according to Amnesty, the government continues to “suppress the rights to freedom of expression, association and peaceful assembly, including through arbitrary detention and prosecutions”. 

The US-Israeli war on Iran has also resulted in a new crackdown from Bahraini authorities, including stripping citizenship from those expressing anything deemed to be supportive of Iran, which has struck targets inside Bahrain.

In his recent call from Jau Prison, Ali described being kept in an overcrowded cell in which half the inmates had to sleep on the floor and in which a lack of ventilation resulted in “suffocating” conditions.

In July, he says he was badly beaten, and he remains “under threat at any moment” from the same “gang”. 

The toilet and washing facilities are unsanitary, he said, with prisoners relying on a hose to wash themselves and overflowing drains.

"Right now, it's just the issue of the Strait of Hormuz. The opening of the Strait of Hormuz is also subject to the fulfillment of the conditions that we announced to the other side," Araghchi said.

"There are conditions from the Supreme Leader, and these conditions must be implemented in order for the Strait of Hormuz to open, and our mission was to convey these conditions to both the American side and all other countries and the international community, so that they are aware that Iran has a plan in this regard.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Ed Miliband confirms UK is considering defying Israeli order to close East Jerusalem consulate
item.description:
Ed Miliband confirms UK is considering defying Israeli order to close East Jerusalem consulate

Submitted by Imran Mulla on Tue, 09/29/2026 - 08:09
The foreign secretary says the UK is ‘looking at all our options’ and discussing the matter with other countries
Britain's Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband speaks on stage on the first day of the annual Labour Party conference in Liverpool, north-west England, on 27 September (AFP)
Off

British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has confirmed the UK government is considering defying the Israeli order to close the British consulate in occupied East Jerusalem, saying “we do not want this to happen”.

The Israeli government ordered the closure of the consulate in retaliation for Miliband’s announcement of sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements earlier this month, giving Britain a deadline of 8 October.

It has previously been assumed that Britain would comply with this Israeli order, but Middle East Eye revealed on Monday that a final decision had not yet been made.

The consulate is in occupied Palestinian territory and Britain recognises the state of Palestine, meaning the UK government does not accept Israel’s order to close the consulate as legitimate.

Foreign Office officials gave an evasive response when approached on Monday morning asking for confirmation that Britain would close the consulate. 

But Miliband addressed the issue in an interview with LBC later that day.

Asked whether the UK could refuse to close the consulate, the foreign secretary said: “We are looking at all our options on this.”

Could Britain defy Israel’s order to shut down its East Jerusalem consulate?

Of the prospect of the consulate in East Jerusalem closing, Miliband insisted: “We do not want this to happen - because it would damage the very important work that we are doing helping people in those communities, including Palestinians.

“The consulate has been there for nearly 200 years, and this is a long-standing position that we have had.”

Miliband condemned the Israeli government’s position, saying: “Morally, it’s completely the wrong thing for them to do.”

Pressed again on what course of action Britain will take, the foreign secretary responded: “I’m going to be circumspect in what I say about this, but we’re looking at all our options.”

He revealed he was talking to foreign ministers around the world about the issue and that the UK’s presence in Jerusalem was “very, very important”.

An act of defiance would almost certainly lead to an enormous diplomatic conflict between Britain and Israel, with tensions already high over the UK’s settlement sanctions.

While it is unlikely that Israeli security would physically remove staff from the premises of the consulate, it can easily block entry to Israel, meaning that British diplomats would be banned from returning to Jerusalem after going on leave.

With Israeli settlers already active in the area around the embassy, there are fears that British diplomats would face harassment, with local staff especially vulnerable.

'Not just wrong, illegal'

Sir Vincent Fean, trustee of the British Palestine Project and himself a former consul-general in East Jerusalem, on Monday told MEE that “Israel’s threat to close the British consulate-general is not just wrong - it is illegal”. 

The British Palestine Project commissioned a legal opinion from Dominic Grieve KC, who served as attorney general under the last Conservative government.

In his opinion, seen by MEE, Grieve says that Israel has made “an unlawful assertion of sovereignty over occupied Palestinian territory. Successive British governments have affirmed that Israel’s rights in East Jerusalem are limited to those of an occupying power.”  

Grieve additionally says that “Israel is asserting a right it does not possess as an occupying power to impose sovereign control over East Jerusalem.”

He notes that the British Mission in East Jerusalem “conducts locally the British government’s relations with the Palestinians. Retaining a consulate-general in East Jerusalem after recognition of the State of Palestine preserves the UK's position that Jerusalem's final status remains to be determined. It does not concede Israeli sovereignty.”

Grieve further notes that British consul generals do not present commissions to Israel, meaning “There is no accreditation to Israel for Israel to withdraw." 

He also warns: “The closure falls on Palestinians, not on Britain alone. Closure threatens consular services, including for British pilgrims, other visitors and residents of Palestine. It hampers aid oversight and reporting from the West Bank and Gaza.”
